query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al-doped CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy coatings, wear performance is governed by the formation of a thin, adherent Al-rich oxide film that acts as a barrier to wear by reducing direct metal-to-metal contact and abrasive damage during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeMnNi HEA coatings without Al addition, which naturally form little to no protective oxide film during wear.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy chemistry by introducing 5–10 at.% Al to the CoCrFeMnNi system and perform controlled sliding wear tests in both oxidizing (ambient air) and inert (argon) environments.
generation.conditions: Conduct sliding wear tests at moderate temperatures (approximately 100–150°C) under fixed loads and consistent sliding speeds, ensuring that the oxidation kinetics are active in air but suppressed in argon.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a thin, adherent Al-rich oxide layer on the coating surface during wear.
generation.mechanism: The Al addition facilitates the formation of a controlled, protective oxide film when exposed to oxygen. This film reduces the direct contact between the wear surfaces, thereby lowering the wear rate by mitigating abrasion. In an inert atmosphere, where oxidation is minimized, the protective effect diminishes, confirming the role of the oxide in wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, the Al-doped HEA coatings will exhibit significantly reduced wear rates and smoother worn surfaces relative to the baseline (undoped) coatings. Under inert conditions, the difference in wear behavior between the Al-doped and baseline coatings will be minimal.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeMnNi HEA coatings without Al addition, which do not form a significant protective oxide layer and exhibit higher wear rates under oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to hold under moderate temperature regimes (100–150°C) where oxidation kinetics are favorable. Extreme conditions such as very high temperatures or environments with negligible oxygen could alter the oxidation behavior and thus the protective mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Al concentration for maximum protection, and how microstructural variations within the coatings may influence oxide formation and stability, remain to be quantified. There is also uncertainty about how the mechanism scales under different temperatures and wear loads.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one set with 5–10 at.% Al added and another baseline set without Al. Conduct identical sliding wear experiments in both ambient air and argon environments at 100–150°C, ensuring constant load and sliding speed.
measurements: Quantify wear rates using weight loss or profilometry measurements
Analyze surface roughness and morphology via SEM
Characterize the presence, thickness, and composition of oxide films using XPS/EDS
Assess microstructural changes with TEM or cross-sectional SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped coatings do not show a significant reduction in wear rates under oxidizing conditions compared to baseline, or if similar oxide film characteristics are observed in both air and argon conditions, then the hypothesis that the protective oxide film governs wear resistance is falsified.

proposals.intervention: Introduce a controlled addition of a larger atomic radius element (e.g., 5–10 at.% Ti) to increase lattice distortion relative to a baseline undoped CoCrFeMnNi composition
proposals.conditions: Conduct wear (pin‐on‐disk) tests at room temperature under identical sliding loads and speeds, ensuring identical processing conditions for both baseline and Ti-doped coatings
proposals.structural_mediator: Degree of lattice distortion and associated changes in dislocation mobility
proposals.mechanism: Increased lattice distortion raises the activation energy for dislocation motion. This suppresses plastic deformation under sliding, yielding higher hardness and reduced wear rate
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the Ti-doped coating should exhibit increased hardness and lower wear loss over a wide range of sliding speeds and loads, with the improvement evident until the distortion becomes detrimental to ductility
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests the hypothesis that the wear performance of HEA coatings is governed by lattice distortion controlling plastic deformation. By introducing an element that accentuates distortion, the change in wear behavior isolates this mechanism from other effects

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA coatings with tailored chemistry
proposals.intervention: Modify the chemistry by adding 5–10 at.% Al to enable the formation of a protective oxide film, in contrast to the baseline CoCrFeMnNi system lacking high oxygen-affinity elements
proposals.conditions: Perform sliding wear tests in both oxidizing (ambient air) and inert (argon atmosphere) conditions at moderate temperatures (~100–150°C) to control oxidation kinetics
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation and stability of a surface oxide layer
proposals.mechanism: Al addition promotes the controlled formation of a thin, adherent oxide film during sliding, which acts as a barrier to wear by reducing direct metal-to-metal contact and mitigating abrasive damage
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, the Al-added coating will show significantly reduced wear rates and smoother worn surfaces compared to the baseline. Under inert conditions, differences should minimize, confirming the role of oxidation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This candidate tests whether wear performance is governed by the reversible formation of protective oxides; a controlled elemental addition and environmental alteration distinguish this mechanism from purely mechanical strengthening

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi HEA coatings under variable mechanical loading
proposals.intervention: Systematically vary the applied normal load during sliding wear tests to induce controlled levels of plastic strain, comparing a baseline low-load regime with a higher load regime
proposals.conditions: Conduct pin‐on‐disk wear experiments across a load range (e.g., from 5 N to 30 N) at constant sliding speed and room temperature while monitoring in situ surface microstructural changes
proposals.structural_mediator: Dynamic formation of nanocrystalline surface layers (or recrystallization) induced by high-shear sliding
proposals.mechanism: At higher loads, the increased shear and plastic deformation can trigger dynamic recrystallization and nanocrystallization at the surface, resulting in a hard, fine-grained layer that retards further wear
proposals.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, a threshold load should exist above which a noticeable nanocrystalline surface layer forms, correlating with an improvement in wear resistance compared to the linear wear progression observed at lower loads; below and above this range, the mechanism’s influence should be quantifiable
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests the idea that wear performance is not solely a function of initial properties but is dynamically controlled by shear-induced microstructural evolution, distinguishing loading effects from static composition influences

proposals.intervention: Apply an annealing treatment in a controlled, low oxygen partial pressure environment to generate a surface compositional gradient, differing from as-deposited homogeneous coatings
proposals.conditions: Subject coatings to annealing at moderate temperatures (e.g., 600–700°C) for a defined time (e.g., 30–60 minutes) under a controlled oxygen atmosphere, followed by wear testing at elevated temperatures representative of service conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Creation of a gradient microstructure with a hard, compositionally graded surface layer due to selective oxidation and elemental partitioning
proposals.mechanism: The controlled anneal promotes selective oxidation and elemental partitioning near the surface, forming a gradient in composition and microstructure that enhances hardness and adhesion of the protective oxide layer, thereby reducing wear
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coatings, the annealed coatings will exhibit a graded hardness profile and improved wear resistance over a range of elevated service temperatures; failure to see a compositional gradient or surface hardening would contradict the mechanism
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction isolates thermal and atmospheric processing as a lever to induce beneficial surface gradients, providing another testable hypothesis for the mechanistic origin of wear resistance in HEA coatings

decision.rationale: Direction C is selected because it directly tests whether the formation of a protective oxide film governs the wear performance of HEA coatings. By introducing 5–10 at.% Al to the CoCrFeMnNi system and comparing wear behavior under oxidizing versus inert atmospheres, the approach clearly isolates the role of controlled oxide formation. The predicted differences in wear behavior between conditions provide a clean baseline-controlled test, making this hypothesis both testable and mechanistically informative.
